vignette:
Elena was thirty-nine years old, a married woman who had spent the last decade working for a small non-profit that provided legal aid to immigrant families in her city. She had always thought of herself as someone who could handle difficult situations, someone who could sit with a client through the worst story and still find the right words. That was before the night that took her words away entirely.

The assault happened in the parking lot behind her office, after a late community meeting. She had been unlocking her car when a man came out of the shadows, holding a tire iron. She remembered the glint of the metal under the single parking lot light, the way he swung it once through the air before using it to smash her driver's side window. What she could not remember, no matter how hard she tried, was the order of anything after that. She knew he had forced her into the back seat. She knew he had made her take off her clothes. She knew he had hurt her. But the sequence was a tangle she could not straighten, and every time she tried to tell a therapist or her husband Carlos what had happened, the words simply would not come. She would open her mouth and find only silence, or fragments that did not connect, and then the rage would rise so fast and so hot that she had to leave the room.

In the weeks that followed, Elena began to change in ways that frightened her. She had always been someone who felt safe in her own skin, but now being naked-even in her own bathroom, even with the door locked-sent her heart racing. She would shower in the dark, or wear a bathing suit under her clothes, because the vulnerability of her own body felt unbearable. At work, she could no longer walk past the supply closet where the office kept a baseball bat for emergencies. The sight of any weapon, even a kitchen knife on her own counter, made her stomach drop. She began to avoid the news, then the street where her office was, then the neighborhood altogether. She told Carlos she was working from home now, which was true for a few weeks, until her supervisor called to say she was running out of sick leave.

What frightened Elena most was what she had come to believe about herself. She was certain now that she was a weak person. Somebody else-somebody stronger, smarter, more alert-would not have let themselves get into that situation. She replayed the meeting that night, the decision to stay late, the choice to park in the back lot. She had failed a basic test of survival, and she could not forgive herself for it. She had also lost something she could not name until she tried to go to her cousin's quinceañera last month. Standing in the church hall, surrounded by the music and the Spanish she had grown up with, she had felt like an imposter. The community that had once held her-the aunts who braided her hair, the neighbors who left extra tamales on her porch-now felt distant, as though a glass wall had come down between her and everyone she loved. She had left the party early, telling herself the noise was too much, but knowing it was something deeper.

Carlos kept telling her she was safe now. The man was in jail. The apartment had new locks. She had nothing to fear. But Elena could not believe him. Her body would not let her. At night, she lay awake listening to every creak and groan of the building, certain that danger lived in the dark hours. During the day, the smallest unexpected sound-a car backfiring, a door slamming-would send her out of her chair, heart pounding, fists clenched. She was jumpy in a way that embarrassed her, and she had started to avoid going out after sunset altogether, which meant she had missed three evening meetings at work and had stopped visiting her mother, who lived only twenty minutes away but whose apartment required walking through a poorly lit parking lot.

It was her mother who finally convinced her to call a clinic. Elena had been crying on the phone, trying to explain why she could not come for dinner, and her mother had said, very quietly, "Mija, you are not the same person. I want my daughter back." Elena had no idea if that person still existed. But she was desperate enough to try. She was afraid of the rage that lived inside her now, afraid of the sleepless nights, afraid of the way her own body felt like a trap. More than anything, she was afraid that she was right-that she really was weak, that she had lost her community forever, that this was who she had become. But she made the call anyway, and she sat in the waiting room with her hands shaking, hoping that someone could help her find the words again.
